title: Matsu's Meaning of the Ancestor's Coming From India
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer encourages listeners to approach meditation with an open and curious mind, allowing themselves to be aware of their thoughts and emotions without attachment or resistance. This involves acknowledging our flaws and imperfections, rather than trying to escape or idealize ourselves, in order to develop acceptance and compassion for ourselves and others. By letting go of our negative tendencies and cultivating a sense of loving-kindness, we can transform our inner "war" into a more peaceful and authentic way of being.

sentences.text: An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.
Morning everyone.
Well, for once, a little bit of good news from our newspaper.

I forget what it was, but in the last day or so, the Supreme Court of the United States, a little surprisingly, by a six to three vote, decided that they would interpret the 1960s civil rights law to include LGBTQ people.
That was surprising.
So they're included as part of the employment discrimination, so that they are not to be discriminated against in issues of employment.
So I don't know exactly what the full implications of this are, or what the pushback will be, or what it will mean exactly, but it sounds like good news and it's certainly cheering.
So today I'm going to bring up another story from Delgan's 300 Koans, case 108, Matsu's Meaning of the Ancestors Coming from India.
Here's the case.
A monastic asked Matsu, aside from the four propositions and the hundred negations, "Please tell me the meaning of the ancestors coming from India."
And Matsu said, "Oh, I'm tired today, and I can't answer your question.
Go ask Jitang."
So the monastic went off and asked Jitang, and Jitang said, "Well, why didn't you ask the master?"
And the monastic said, "Well, I did.
I asked him, but he told me to ask you."
And Jitang said, "Oh, I have a headache today, and I can't answer your question.
Why don't you go ask Bajong?"
So the monastic went off and he asked Bajong the same question.
And Bajong said, "Having gotten to this point, I don't understand it."
So the monastic went back to Matsu and he told him what had happened.
And Matsu said, "Jitang's head is white, Bajong's head is black."
Another great story.
So what are we looking for in our practice?
I think I was saying yesterday that we strive for goodness inside and out.
We believe in goodness, even if maybe in a sober moment we kind of have to admit perhaps it's impossible.
It doesn't matter.
We believe in it.
We strive for it.
And we can't help ourselves but to do that because we're built like that.
So today I want to say that we are also built to strive for truth.
What is truth anyway?
It's kind of a crazy concept.
Maybe you can tell the difference between the truth and a lie when you speak something or hear someone speak something.
You could say that that's true or that's not true because it accords with the facts as we know them or it does not accord with the facts.
But the truth itself, what is truth?
How could anything not be true?
I always feel like people are always telling me the truth and the whole truth.
Even when they're lying to me, they are telling me the truth about who they are and how things are.
Because they are there in front of me, completely expressing themselves fully and truthfully.
How could they do anything otherwise?
And if I open my eyes, I see this.
And it's true.
If we open our eyes and we look around, anything we see, everything we see, anyone we see is the truth.
What truth could there be beyond this?
Still, it's an ancient idea in all cultures that there is a false world and there is a true world.
And somehow this is, again, something that is unique to us as human beings.
It's something that we feel, that we can be true to ourselves or not.
We can be authentic or not.
Our lives can be real or they can be unreal.

The ancient Greek philosophers thought that this world in which things come and go, in which there are so many problems, in which things constantly break, people constantly betray one another or hurt and oppress one another, this world must be a false world.
And behind this world there must be a true world that philosophers should strive to discover and that they could discover through reason and reflection and meditation.
They could discover a true world behind this corrupt world.
And although the Buddha didn't really worry too much about truth, in fact in some ways you could say the Buddha was against truth.
He opposed it.
Still, the Buddha was concerned with suffering in the end of suffering, which is maybe only a slightly different idea of what's the truth.
Samsara and nirvana, two different worlds.
To find a path of you, a way to end suffering rather than to stay stuck in suffering, maybe this is the Buddha's equivalent of the path of truth.

In any case, it sure seems like for us human beings, unlike for other animals and other living things, who may in some very important ways be a lot smarter and better adjusted to the planet Earth than we are, it's not enough to just live the life we're given.
Somehow we think we have to go beyond it.
Somehow we think we have to find the truth.
So I think however ridiculous it may be, and the Zen masters are always pointing out what a trap it is, still we want to find the truth.
And that's what this monastic in the story is looking for.
"Show me the truth.
Why did Bodhidharma come from the West?"
It means what is the truth of our practice?
What is this about?
But of course, as this monastic is finding out in the story, it's a problem.
As soon as we find the truth, it's no longer the truth.
As soon as we grab truth, it seems to disappear in our hands.
Still, we have to look for it, we have to strive for it.
The monk, the monastic in the story has to ask.
There's no story if he or she doesn't ask.
And in our sitting, I think we should be looking for the truth.
We should sit peacefully if we can, as best we can, letting go of whatever comes to heart or mind.
Aware, let go, aware, let go.
Come back to the breath, return to silence.
But at the same time, there should be a sense of striving in our sitting.
There should be a search for something beyond our usual mind.
We should be on a quest for truth, even if we know that it's an impossible quest.
So we sit on our cushion, and whether we use the words or don't use the words, we sit with a sense of, "What is it?
Who is this?
What is this human life?
What is the truth of truths?"
And we have to really ask in all sincerity, even though we know we can't find some truth.
But maybe, for a moment, we do find some truth that slips through our fingers.
And we're there for it.
Or maybe, even better, we're not there for it.
The other day I mentioned Anam Thukten's great book, *Choosing Compassion*.
It's a simple, short, beautiful book.
And I was reading in that book, he talks about the mind of disenchantment.
Disenchantment.
That's the mind we find, he says, when we are willing to be honest enough to look within and see the deep-seated patterns of our mind.
To look and see the habitual tendencies of greed, hate, and delusion.
Our own special and particular way we have of messing ourselves up, making trouble for our friends, and contributing to this big mess we call the world.
The mind of disenchantment, because usually our mind is enchanted by itself.
And this is kind of a funny, counter-intuitive way of thinking about it.
Because usually we don't feel like we're enchanted.
Our mind feels pretty dull, usually.
Stupid.
We're very unaware and kind of crashing around.

But Anam is suggesting that actually, although it may feel ordinary and dull to us, the truth is we are enchanted by our minds in the way that a crowd is enchanted by a magician or a patient is put into trance by a mesmerist.
What we take to be our usual everyday mind is really a mind enchanted by the shiny things we want and the shiny things we don't want.
It's a mind entranced by the suffering of its culture and family lineage.
A mind mesmerized by its own suffering that it chases and chases like a dog chasing its tail.
And the mind of disenchantment arises when we are willing to stop just chasing reflexively and turn around and look and see.
"This is my mind.
This is how it is.
These are the ways I'm habituated and conditioned to really feel it, really take it in."
Maybe with one conscious breath we can break the spell and actually see what's going on.
And I think we don't want to do this because it's not too much fun.
It's not too much fun to recognize how tied into knots we are.
Right away we're tempted to be enchanted all over again by whatever comes to hand.
Self-judgment, that would be good.
This very shiny and compelling thought, "I should be better.
I don't like this way I am.
I'm not a very good, very attractive person.
Other people are so much better than me."
As soon as I believe all that I'm back immediately into my trance, which is so familiar.
Or maybe we are enchanted by some other mind that we imagine we could be having if only we didn't have this crappy one.
This wonderful mind that we will have someday when our practice really starts working.
So to just be disenchanted, to be with our mind as it really is, doesn't feel like too much fun.
It seems kind of uninspiring.
But this really is the main practice that we have to do.
Just to be aware in our whole body, not just in our ideas, but in our whole body to be aware of the patterns of our mind.
Sitting a little bit like we're doing this week, maybe we see our patterns over and over again.
Maybe in this sense it's actually good that we're in our own houses where it's more likely that these patterns will be coming up all the time.

Maybe being in our own houses it helps us to overcome the illusion which might also entrance us that Session at Samish Island is so great and so inspiring and so beautiful to get away from it all and be here in this big sky, big space.
That's the place and only there that we can get beyond ourselves.
And then we have our last circle.
We say goodbye and we go home, back to the usual trance, back to the usual grind.
Well now we don't have that illusion anymore because here we are in our house where all the things that are embedded with our usual mind are all around us.
Maybe it's discouraging to see our mind playing its usual tricks, but also it can be quite amusing.
"This is how I am.
Wow, in all the heavens and below the earth no one else is crazy in just this way."
It can be quite nice actually to look at a fire, especially at that quieter time when the fire is banked down a bit and you see the glowing coals that seem so benign and they're warm.
If you don't keep adding fuel to the fire and making it blaze up until it rages out of control and if you don't stick your hand in the fire, a fire can be nice.
There are times when you look into your own mind and you feel terrified.
Annam brings this up in his book.
You can be terrified of your own mind that there could be in it so much violence, so much anger.
In fact, whatever you see in the world that you fear or dislike that really, really bothers you, you can rest assured that very thing is in your own mind.
And it can be terrifying to realize that this is you.
This is your mind.
You are human, a very powerful and disturbing condition to have to bear.
Annam tells the story of his relationship to his teacher, Lama Tsurlo, who he says was a very gentle and kind person.
Annam always wanted to spend time with him, but at the same time he was really scared of him.
He said, "It didn't make sense for me to be scared of Lama Tsurlo.
He was so sweet and kind.
He never was mean to me or abusive to me in any way.
So how come I'm so scared of him?"
And he finally saw that the reason he was scared was because he imagined that the Lama was so wise and so enlightened that he would be able to see right through him.
He would be able to see into his mind and see what a mass of confusion and afflictive emotions he actually was inside, even though on the outside he was very nice and looked good and everything.
And that's why he was afraid of his teacher.
It was the sort of fear, Annam says, that you have when a very important person is coming over to your house to visit and your house is a total mess.
And you want the person to come, but you really are so frightened because you don't want them to see how you live, so messy and everything.
So you're excited and happy, but also terrified.
So ultimately Annam realized that the reason he was afraid of his Lama was that he was afraid of his own mind.
He was afraid to face all the fear and all the anger that he had inside himself.
And he thought he was doing a really good job of hiding it from everyone, including maybe especially himself, but that the Lama would know that it was there.
And you know, probably it's true that the Lama would be able to see Annam's mess through the smooth exterior.

But probably not because the Lama was an enlightened mind reader, but because when you are aware and accepting of your own mess, you are then willing to accept it and you have some kind of basic intuition.
You can see how other people are also a mess because you understand that they're just like you.
It's a little bit like an alcoholic in recovery who has an unerring ability to recognize other alcoholics more than other people can.
And I think this is true of all of us.
We don't want everyone else to know what a mess we are.
And the person we really don't want to know is ourselves because it's just too awful, it's just too embarrassing.
So actually we're scared of one another, all other people, not just Lamas, because we're scared that somehow they might be able to see through us.
And when you think about it, although maybe it's funny to say, in a way we're all always a little bit wary of one another.
Don't we try to make ourselves look good when we meet another person?
Maybe that's one nice thing about the Zoom era.
We can stay in our pajamas all day.
We don't need to fancy ourselves up.
Somehow or other it takes the edge off our need to impress each other with our shiny selves.
And yet we're still there.
We're still there.
We can't escape from ourselves because although the other people are not in our presence, we are.
And maybe one great thing about our sitting, very prosaic, not very spiritual, but it's a great thing.
It gives us a chance to be honest with ourselves and to get used to our own craziness.
So we should not have great expectations for ourselves that we're going to be kind, wise, wonderful people that the world will celebrate.
Probably that's not going to happen.
Probably we're going to be a mess forever and ever.
Of course we will.
As long as there's one person anywhere who's a mess, we're a mess.
So we should be okay with that.
We should not condemn ourselves for it.
We should be always forgiving ourselves for it.
But we also should not be sloppy with our conduct of body, speech, and mind.
In other words, even though we know we're a pathetic human being, we're not kidding ourselves or anybody else, let's do our best to be decent.
We don't need to act or speak with unkindness.
When we sit, we see our mind coming and going like clouds in the sky.
Once in a while, too, we even see a bit of pure blue that shatters the scene.
But the clouds are also beautiful.
Sitting this way, we get used to our messed up minds.
We get used to being human.
When we're used to it, we can accept it.
And then we will not be afraid of others.
We can be at ease all the time with others when we do not have any longer the pressure to prove to them and ourselves that we are something other than we are.
Anam in his chapter tells the story that I think I had heard before.
I bet you've heard it before, too.
I think it's a Native American story about a grandfather who says to his grandson, "There's a war going on inside me."
And the grandson says, "Who's fighting?"
And the grandfather answers, "There are two wolves fighting.
The bad wolf, full of anger, fear, and clinging and grasping, and the good wolf, who's loving, wise, and open-hearted."
And boy, it's an ugly battle.
And the grandson says, "Which one will win?"
And the grandfather says, "The one I feed the most."
So we will always have this war going on inside us.
And that's why we pay attention to our mind wisely and carefully so that we know what to do.
Luckily, we have precepts, we have teachings, we have one another, and we have our own familiarity with our own minds.
So we know what it feels like to be stuck in our negativity, our self-protectiveness.
It feels lousy.
It feels confining.
So we don't want to get stuck on our negativity.
So when we feel it, we know we're feeling it.
We let go.
And when we can't let go and we do get stuck, we know we're stuck.
We know this is what it feels like when I'm stuck.
Not too good.
And we're clear that whatever is going on right now, our commitment not to be stuck is the commitment of a lifetime.
So we may feel it, but we don't feed it.
We don't believe all the thoughts of blaming and anger and so on that will strengthen our bitterness.
These thoughts and emotions may come, but we recognize them and we stay patient with them.
We don't feed the grasping, angry wolf.
We feed the loving, open-hearted wolf.
Every time we sit, every time we chant, every time we bow, every time we're kind, every time we let go, every time we forgive,
we are feeding and strengthening this good wolf, this good human mind.

Just to be kind to ourselves for a moment, to strengthen our good human mind, our nice, fluffy, maybe like Alaskan white wolf so that we do that as much as we can, staying open with our mind, accepting our mind, forgiving ourselves over and over again.
We can't help being who we are.
We can't help being human beings.
We were born this way, but we know what in ourselves to encourage and what in ourselves to just let be.

Anam quotes James Baldwin, one of the most eloquent writers we have, who said famously, "I imagine one of the reasons why people cling to their hate so stubbornly is because once the hate is gone, they'll be forced to deal with their pain."
I'm not sure, but probably he was talking about white people, especially white people he saw when he was growing up who really seemed to have a strong antipathy toward black people.
And it's funny that Baldwin, who was a black gay man, understood these white people probably much better than they understood themselves.

And one of the deepest aspects of racism in America that we're now beginning to feel finally is the pain and the guilt white people have probably always been avoiding, covering it up with all kinds of hatred, arrogance, disrespect, thoughtlessness, so that they didn't need to feel it, to have been perpetrators and beneficiaries of such crimes.
Who could bear this?
Who could bear the pain and the guilt?
And this is true in the widest possible way.
All anger, hatred, and self-denigration is actually a protection for the ego.
We think it's an attack on the ego, but it's a protection for the ego.

All afflictive emotion is in the end a distraction from the pain we feel because we are vulnerable human beings and we are going to die soon, and the guilt we feel because we're all separate from each other.
And none of us can claim that we've loved enough.
And this separation is built into the structure of our consciousness.
When you think about it, that's actually the definition of consciousness, separation.
I can't be conscious of something unless I am not that thing.
Mind is over here, object is over there, that's what defines consciousness.
The vision, cutting the cat in two, a very violent and destructive act in its nature.
And consciousness is inherently critical because it is inherently in exile from itself, and so it is straining towards something.
And every object is subject to discrimination and critique.
Every object either meets my approval or my disapproval.
Rather than just let objects come and go as they naturally will, my mind must critique them.
Some objects it wants to keep hold of because they're good and I like them, others I want to get rid of because they're bad, they're unpleasant to me.
And in this way, we're at war because we want pleasure, we don't want pain.
We want to live, we don't want to die.
And we have all sorts of preferences and aversions based on our conditioning and our history.
We like this kind of person, we don't like that kind of person.
We try to realize our preferences, to get what we prefer and get rid of what we would prefer to get rid of.
We want to be with the people we're attracted to.
We want to avoid the people we don't think we like, who frighten us.
And in this way, drop by drop by drop, we build an ocean of suffering in a fractured and painful world.
And we never could help it to begin with.
Of course, this is what we have done.
And when we're willing, finally, to really see how painful all this is, and to understand the real source of the pain, our heart wants to put together what has been torn apart.
We realize the self-defensive nature of all our critique, really there's nothing to prefer.
How superficial are all our preferences and critiques.
Deeper in us is the desire for the truth of all things, oneness in love.
Now we come back to our story.
I was saying that although we don't find truth because there's nothing to find, we can't help but seek truth.
Beyond our preferences for this or that thing or this or that state of mind or heart is simply our deep desire for the truth, the oneness of things, and for love.
But you can't find it.
How could you find it?
Because if you could find it, you would be separate from it.
You would critique it.
It would disappear.
Since you are it, you can't find it.
That's why nobody answers the monastics' question.
But they don't want to be discouraging, so they send them on to the next one, so that he can hear from many angles and many voices lovingly teaching him the truth.
So today and in others of my talks, I've been trying a little bit, the best I can,
to say some words about racism because it's so important now.
It always has been, but now we know.
So it's funny, actually, that in this Zen story I'm bringing up today, it talks about black and white, right?
Did you notice that?
Black and white.
I think it's unlikely that in the story the black and the white refers to skin color.
Not impossible, but unlikely.
I don't think also it refers to hair color because the monastics shaved their head.
The commentaries always say that in this story white and black stands for Dharma position.
In other words, a specific and unique manifestation of the truth of impermanence, of emptiness, of awakening.
Sometimes in Zen we call it just this.
Sometimes we call it suchness.
The heart yearns for awakening.
Certainly it's the center of the Buddhist path, and yet it's so slippery and impossible.
You can't define it.
It doesn't look like this or that.
It doesn't have characteristics or marks.
It isn't caused by anything.
It's unconditioned by definition.
And yet it appears right in front of us, all of a sudden, as this or that.
The entire truth flashes right in front of us, in and out of existence.
Dogen calls this Genjokoan.
Matsu tells us sometimes it appears as Bai Zhong, sometimes it appears as Qi Tang, and yes, sometimes it appears as Matsu, sometimes it appears as the monastic.
I guess probably Bai Zhong and Qi Tang were very different kinds of people.
Who knows, maybe they were even from different racial groups, because there were different racial groups represented in the Chinese Sangha.
In China, we think of Chinese people, but China has a million different ethnic groups.
I think we're getting to know that now as the Han Chinese are suppressing different ethnic groups.
Anyway, whatever the differences were or weren't between Bai Zhong and Qi Tang, there is in the end nothing to be said about them.
Because each one, as he is, is what he is, the whole truth.
Each one, each appearance, each moment, each appearance in each moment is the whole of the truth.
If we're looking for the truth, we always find it right here in seeing, in hearing, in feeling, in thinking.
So we come to today.
How did that happen?
I'm always so confused.
Honestly, I've been in my house, you know, and nowhere else virtually at all for three months now.
Where does every day go?
I'm asking you, where?
Where does it go?
I can't understand.
And we have come to, I think, unless I'm mistaken, is the last full day of our sesshin.
We're sitting all of today and tomorrow, not the whole day.
So today's the last day we have to experience in the context of sesshin, morning, late morning, afternoon, late afternoon, early evening, later evening, and nighttime, and sleep.
So let's make the best of this unique, special, really important, and crucial day.
Thank you all very much for being here.
Thank you for listening to my talk.
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place, with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
